source: Cox & D'Antonio 3e Table 6.9, PDF page 262 (printed p. 205)
about: Rendered PDF page 262, folio 205 (running head "Porous sound absorption 205"); the table fills the whole page and nothing else is printed on it. Title as printed: "Table 6.9 Example tortuosity values from the literature". Two columns, headings in italic: "Material" and "Tortuosity". Tortuosity is dimensionless and the page prints no unit, so every number is carried over as it stands. Four bold section headings divide the body, "Fibrous materials", "Cellular materials", "Granular materials" and "Other", and they are kept as the group field; the first two are plural here and singular in Table 6.8. Thin horizontal rules are also drawn inside the groups, a typographic aid only. There are no footnotes and no empty cells. Six rows carry no superscript and so have no attributed_to: "Common fibrous absorbents, e.g., rock wool", "Poroelastic foam", "Loose sand or dry cultivated soil", "Granular materials", "Snow (new)" and "Snow (old crusted)". Cells printed as a bare en dash interval go to ranges, including the two that start at a whole number, "1–1.06" and "1–1.6", and "2–3.3". Cells that list several values or several intervals separated by a comma go to reported and the scalar field is left out: Plastic foam "1.06 and 1.7", Rubber crumb "1.13–1.26, 1.38–1.56", Vermiculite "1.48–1.58, 1.8–2.46" and Nitrile foam granulate "1.31, 1.49". Only one lead shot row is printed here, "Lead shot", where Table 6.8 splits the same material into "2.1 mm lead shot" and "4 mm lead shot". Two things worth knowing about this page. First, the PDF text layer of the book ends the table at the "Snow" row, but the rendered page prints two further rows below it, "Snow (new)" 1.5–2.7 and "Snow (old crusted)" 4, and both are transcribed here; the table therefore has 37 rows. Second, "Cellular rubber" sits under Granular materials on this page while Table 6.8 lists it under Cellular material, and "Poroelastic foam" carries superscript 65 in Table 6.8 but no superscript at all here. The prose that introduces the table (PDF page 261, printed p. 204, just below Table 6.8) reads "Real absorbents, however, are not normally that well ordered. Consequently, tortuosity needs to be measured. Techniques for doing this are discussed in Chapter 4. Some values are given in Table 6.9. Another approach is to calculate the tortuosity from the structure of the material at a microscopic scale.23,82,86,89", and the preceding section defines tortuosity as the effect of pore orientation on sound propagation, denoted α∞, noting that "Some older publications used the term structural form factor, and there were some differences in the definition." As in Table 6.8, the superscript on "Perlite" is 5, and reference 5 of chapter 6 is a Wikimedia Commons photograph credit (Siim Sepp, "Sand from Gobi Desert", licensed CC BY-SA 3.0, accessed 3 May 2015), not a source of measured tortuosity; the credit is recorded as the page prints it.
